name: Dorsal scapular nerve
summary: The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root (with a C4 contribution) above the upper trunk, pierces the scalenus medius and descends along the medial border of the scapula deep to the levator scapulae and the rhomboids, which it supplies. Because it leaves the root before the plexus forms, rhomboid weakness distinguishes a C5 root lesion from an upper trunk lesion, and its EMG is one of the tests that places a lesion at the root: a C5 radiculopathy denervates the rhomboids, whereas Erb palsy of the upper trunk spares them. It is entrapped in the scalenus medius, producing interscapular pain and scapular winging in a pattern different from that of the long thoracic nerve.

anatomy.location: Leaves the C5 anterior ramus in the neck, pierces the scalenus medius, runs beneath the levator scapulae along the medial scapular border with the dorsal scapular artery, deep to the rhomboid minor and major, which it supplies together with the levator scapulae.

function: Motor to the levator scapulae and the rhomboids, it elevates and retracts the scapula and stabilizes it during arm movement; its loss produces mild lateral winging of the scapula with the inferior angle displaced laterally (the opposite direction from serratus anterior weakness), difficulty bracing the shoulders back and a dull interscapular ache. Its origin proximal to the plexus makes it a root marker: rhomboid denervation on EMG with deltoid and biceps weakness means the C5 root or a preganglionic avulsion (a poor prognosis for repair), whereas spared rhomboids mean a postganglionic upper trunk injury that may regenerate. Entrapment in the scalenus medius accompanies neck trauma and thoracic outlet syndromes.

imaging.normalAppearance: A small nerve piercing the scalenus medius and running beneath the levator scapulae on ultrasound; routine MRI shows only its muscles, which show denervation edema or fatty atrophy.

pathology.finding: Denervation of the rhomboids with the deltoid, biceps and supraspinatus; a pseudomeningocele on myelography or MRI marks a root avulsion.
STIR hyperintensity and later fatty atrophy of the rhomboids and levator scapulae with a normal serratus anterior.
Denervation of deltoid, biceps and supraspinatus with normal rhomboids, placing the lesion distal to the root.

lesionEffects.deficit: Lateral scapular winging and weak scapular retraction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Denervation of the rhomboids and levator scapulae

lesionEffects.deficit: Marker of C5 root (versus upper trunk) lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Origin of the nerve proximal to the plexus

examination: Ask the patient to brace the shoulders back against resistance and watch for lateral displacement of the inferior scapular angle

pearls: Rhomboids weak means the lesion is at the C5 root; rhomboids strong means the trunk
